parole.significato: -th (forms an ordinal number from a cardinal number)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -ēnus.

parole.significato: forms the infinitive of the third-conjugation verbs
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese -ir, from Latin -īre, the ending of the present active infinitive form of fourth conjugation verbs. In some verbs, it is a reflex of Latin -ere of the third conjugation.
Learned borrowing from Latin -īvus. Doublet of -io.
From Old Galician-Portuguese abrir, from Latin aperīre, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epo (“off, from”) + *wer-iō (“open”).
Learned borrowing from Latin accidentem, present active participle of accidō (“happen”); from ad (“to”) + cadō (“fall”); respectively from Proto-Indo-European *ád (“near, at”) and *ḱad- (“to fall”).

parole.significato: mallard (Anas platyrhynchos, a wild species of duck)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ãade, from Latin anatem (“duck”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énh₂t-.

parole.significato: someone else’s, that belongs to someone else
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese alhẽo, from Latin aliēnus ("belonging to someone else", later "exotic, foreign"), from alius (“other”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élyos. Compare Galician alleo, Spanish ajeno. Doublet of alien.

parole.significato: terrace (platform that extends outwards from a building)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin appendere (“to hang”), from ap- + pendō (“to hang”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pend- (“to pull; to spin”).

parole.significato: air layering, marcottage (developing a new plant from the branch of a tree)
parole.testo: From Latin porca (“balk”), from Proto-Indo-European *pr̥ḱeh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *perḱ- (“to dig”). Even though the word starts with "al", it is not a prefix, but rather an adaptation of Portuguese alporque (“swelling, scrofula”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese alto, from Latin altus, ultimately of Proto-Indo-European origin. This form is likely a semi-learned term, or was influenced by learned elements of the language and uses such an orthography, as with Galician and Spanish alto (which have popularly inherited variants outo
From alvo (“white”), from Latin albus (“white”), from Proto-Indo-European *albʰós (“white”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese ambos, from Latin ambōs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂m̥bʰi (“round about, around”).
Learned borrowing from Latin angulāris (“angular”), from angulus (“corner; angle”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂engulos.
Borrowed from Latin anteriōrem.

parole.significato: plough (device pulled through the ground to open furrows)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese arado, from Latin arātrum, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂érh₃trom.
From Latin armāmentum (“equipment”), from arma (“weapon”) (from Proto-Indo-European *h₂(e)rmos (“fitting”)) + -mentum (from Proto-Indo-European *-men- and *-nteh₂-).
Inherited from Latin artem (“practical skill”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂r̥tís (“fitting”), from the root *h₂er- (“to join”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin āctus, perfect passive participle of agō (“to make, I do”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eǵ- (“to lead”). Doublet of ato.
From Old Galician-Portuguese bel, from Latin bellus, from Proto-Indo-European *dw-ene-, adverbial form of *deu- (“to do, perform, revere, show favor”).
Probably a borrowing from Latin brevis (“short”) (compare Spanish breve, where *brieve would be expected if the term were inherited), from Proto-Indo-European *mréǵʰus.

parole.significato: crosier (staff of a bishop or abbot)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin baculum, from Proto-Indo-European *bak-.
From Latin callum (“callus”), from Proto-Indo-European *kal (“hard”).

Borrowed from Latin cancellāre (“to make like a lattice, to cover with a lattice, to cancel”), ultimately from cancer (“lattice, grid”), from Proto-Indo-European *geng- (“lump”). Doublet of chancelar, via French.
From Latin caput (“head”), from Proto-Indo-European *kauput-.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese caridade, from Latin cāritātem (“dearness, charity”), from cārus (“dear”), from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ros.
From Old Galician-Portuguese caro, from Latin cārus (“dear, beloved”), from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ros.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese carpir, from Latin carpere (“to tear off”), from Proto-Indo-European *kerp- (“to pluck, harvest”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese carvon, from Latin carbōnem. Doublet of carbono.
From Old Galician-Portuguese casa, from Latin casa (“cottage”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *kat- (“to link or weave together; chain, net; hut, shed”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese castro, from Latin castrum, from Proto-Indo-European *kes- (“to cut, cut off, separate”). Cognate with Galician and Spanish castro. Doublet of alcácer, via Arabic.

parole.significato: stem (part of the axis of a plant, which normally supports the leaves)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caulis. Doublet of couve.
From Old Galician-Portuguese cela (“cell”), from Latin cella (“small room”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelnā.

parole.significato: rye (grass or its grains as food)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese centẽo (“rye”), from Latin centēnus (“a hundred things”), from Latin centum (“a hundred”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm. Cognate with Galician centeo, and Spanish centeno. Doublet of Centeno.
From Old Galician-Portuguese certo, from Latin certus (“certain”), past participle of cernō (“to sift; to discern”), from Proto-Indo-European *krey- (“to move; to separate”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese cervo, from Latin cervus (“deer, stag”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥h₂wós, from *ḱerh₂- (“horn”). Cognate with Galician cervo, Spanish ciervo, Catalan cérvol, Occitan cèrvi, French cerf, Italian cervo and Romanian cerb.

parole.significato: sore (injured, infected, inflamed, or diseased patch of skin)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese chaga (“sore”), from Latin plāga (“injury”), from plangō (“strike”), from Proto-Indo-European *plak-. Compare Galician chaga, Spanish llaga, French plaie, Italian piaga, Romanian plagă, Catalan plaga, and more distantly with Ancient Greek πληγή (plēgḗ, “wound”)
From Old Galician-Portuguese chama, from Latin flamma, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlē- (“to shimmer, gleam, shine”). Cognate with Galician chama, and Spanish llama. Doublet of flama.

parole.significato: cane (slender flexible stem of plants such as bamboo)
parole.testo: From Latin culmus, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱolh₂mos.

parole.significato: colonist (a founder or member of a colony)
parole.testo: From Latin colōnus (“farmer; colonist”), from colō (“till, cultivate, worship”), from earlier * quelō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- (“to move; to turn (around)”).

parole.significato: colony (geographical area under the remote control of a country)
parole.testo: From Latin colōnia (“colony”), from colōnus (“farmer; colonist”), from colō (“till, cultivate, worship”), from earlier * quelō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- (“to move; to turn (around)”).

parole.significato: common; frequent (occurring often or existing in many places)
parole.testo: From Latin commūnis (“common, public, general”) from Proto-Indo-European *ḱom-moyn-is (“held in common”).
Borrowed from Latin concēdere (“to give way, to yield, to grant, to allow”), from con- (“wholly”) + cēdō (“to yield, give way, to go, grant”), from Proto-Indo-European *ked- (“to go, yield”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese coor f, from Latin colōrem m, from Old Latin colos (“covering”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover, conceal”). Doublet of color. Compare Galician cor and Spanish color.

parole.significato: horn (growth on the heads of certain animals)
parole.testo: From Latin cornū, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (“horn”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese corpo, from Latin corpus, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱrep-. Doublet of the borrowings corpus and cós.
From Old Galician-Portuguese cortiça, from Latin corticea, feminine of corticeus (“of cork, of bark”), from cortex (“bark, cork”), from Proto-Indo-European *ker-, *sker- (“cut”). Doublet of cortíceo.

parole.significato: several leaf vegetables, from the family Brassica oleracea
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese couve, from earlier *coue, from Latin caulem (“stem of a cabbage”), from Ancient Greek καυλός (kaulós, “stem”). Doublet of caule.

parole.significato: crust (any solid, hard surface layer; outer layer of bread and pastry)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Latin crusta, from Proto-Indo-European *krustós (“hardened”), from *krews- (“to form a crust, begin to freeze”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cuu (“ass”), from Latin cūlum. Compare Galician cu, Spanish and Italian culo, French cul, and Romanian cur.

From Old Galician-Portuguese cujo, from Latin cuius, a genitive of quī (“which”) which had been used adjectivally since at least the time of Plautus. cp. Ancient Greek ποῖος (poîos), both from Proto-Indo-European *kʷís.

parole.significato: cure (a method, device or medication that restores good health)
parole.testo: From Latin cūra, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeys- (“to heed”).
From curar (“to cure”), from Latin curō, from Proto-Indo-European *koys- (“to care for, cure”). By surface analysis, curar + -eiro.

parole.significato: short (having a small distance between ends or edges)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese curto, corto, from Latin curtus, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-, *(s)k(ʷ)Art-, *(s)k(ʷ)Ard- (“short”).
Borrowed from Latin curvus (“bent”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn; to bend”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese can, from Latin canis, canem. Compare Galician and Spanish can.
Learned borrowing from Latin celerem.
Learned borrowing from Latin cilium, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel-yo-m, which is derived from *ḱel- (“to cover”). Doublet of celha.
Borrowed from Latin cortex.
Inherited from Latin cumulus (“mound”). Doublet of cúmulo.
Borrowed from Latin concavus (“concave”), cōn + cavus (“hollow”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱówHwos (“cavity”), from *ḱówH-.

parole.significato: digit, a part of the body inclusive of fingers or toes
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dedo, from Latin digitus, from Proto-Indo-European *deyǵ- (“to show, point out, pronounce solemnly”). Doublet of dígito, which was borrowed. Compare Galician dedo, Spanish dedo, and Catalan dit.
From Latin dēmittere (“to bring down”), from de (“from, away from, down from”) + mittō (“send; emit; throw, cast”), from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange, remove”).
Learned borrowing from Latin dēnsus.
From des- + ligar, from Latin ligāre (“to bind”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵ- (“to bind”). Doublet of desliar.
From Latin differentia (“difference”), from differō (“to differ”), from dif- + ferō (“to carry”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to bear, carry”).

From Latin difficultātem (“difficulty”), from difficilis (“difficult, troublesome”), from dis- (“not”) + facilis (“easy”, whence Portuguese fácil), from faciō (“to do, to make”, whence Portuguese fazer), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to do, put, place, set”, root of English do).
Borrowed from Latin diffūsus (“diffused”), perfect passive participle of diffundō (“to diffuse”), dif- + fundō (“to pour out”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰew-.

Modified from learned form directo, borrowed from Latin dīrēctus (“straight”), from dīrigō (“lay straight; direct; distribute”), from dis- + regō (“to rule, to govern”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ-. Compare the inherited direito.
Borrowed from Latin discernere (“to separate, divide, distinguish, discern”), from dis- (“apart”) + cernere (“to separate”), from Proto-Indo-European *krey-.

Borrowed from Latin dissertātiōnem (“spoken dissertation”), from dissertus (“explained”), from disserō (“to arrange or explain”), from dis- + serō (“to spread, to scatter”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind, put together”).

parole.significato: dictatorship (a government led by a dictator)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dictātūra, dictātor (“chief magistrate”), from dictō (“to dictate, to prescribe”), from dīcō (“to say, to speak”), Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ-e- (“to show, point out”).

parole.significato: domestic (of or relating to the home)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin domesticus (“domestic”), from domus (“house”), from Proto-Indo-European *dṓm.

parole.significato: during (for all of a given time interval)
parole.testo: From Latin dūrantem (“enduring”), from dūrō (“last, endure”), from dūrus (“hard”), from Proto-Indo-European *deru-, *drew- (“hard, fest”).

parole.significato: debt (action, state of mind, or object one has an obligation to perform for another, adopt toward another, or give to a…
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese divida, devida, deveda, from Latin dēbita, plural of dēbitum, from dēbitus (“owed”), from dēbeō (“to owe”), from dē + habeō (“to have”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeh₁bʰ- (“to grab, to take”). Doublet of débito.

parole.significato: axle, axletree (the pin or spindle on which a wheel revolves)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese eixe, from Latin axis (“axletree”) (with change of declension), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs- (“axis”). Compare Galician eixe, Spanish eje. Doublet of the borrowing áxis.
From Old Galician-Portuguese *ãelo, from Latin ānellus, diminutive of anus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eh₂no- (“ring”). See also the doublet anel, borrowed from Occitan.

parole.significato: emission (something that is emitted, especially the exhaust from a car)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēmissiōnem (“sending forth”), from ēmittō (“send out”), from ex (“from, out of”) + mittō (“send”), from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange, remove”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese encoller, from en- (“in-”) + coller (“collect”), from Latin colligō (“to collect”), from con- + legō (“to bring together, to gather, to collect”), from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-.
From encruzilhar (“to cross”), from cruz (“cross”), from Old Galician-Portuguese cruz, from Latin crux (“cross”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, to bend”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese enfermo, from Latin īnfirmus (“sick, feeble”), from in- + firmus (“firm”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer-mo-s (“holding”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese anguia, Latin anguīllam, presumably in a form *anguīlam, to account for the elision of the /l/. Cognate with Spanish anguila.

parole.significato: among (denotes a mingling or intermixing with distinct or separable objects)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese entre, antre, from Latin inter (“between; among”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁enter (“between”).
From Latin involvere (“to involve”), from in (“in, at, on”) + volvō (“to roll”), from Proto-Indo-European *wel- (“to turn, wind, round”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese suffre (with the prefix en-), from Latin sulfur, sulphur, suphure, from Proto-Indo-European *swelplos, from the root *swel- (“to burn, smoulder”). Compare Galician xofre and Spanish azufre. Doublet of súlfur.
PIE word  *nókʷts From Latin aequinoctium (“equinox”), from aequus (“equal”) + nox (“night”) (ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts (“night”)) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns).
From Old Galician-Portuguese erva, from Latin herba, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow, become green”). Cognate with Galician herba and Spanish hierba.

parole.significato: writing (written letters or symbols that express some meaning)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese escrita, from Latin scrīpta, feminine form of scrīptus (“written”), from scrībō (“to write”), from Proto-Indo-European *skreybʰ-.

From Old Galician-Portuguese escudo (“shield”), from Latin scūtum (“shield”), from Proto-Indo-European *skei- (“to cut, split”), which is an extension of *sek- (“to cut”). The name of the currency comes from the heraldic shields on the coins.

parole.significato: to scatter, to strew, to spread
parole.testo: From Latin spargō (“scatter”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pregʰ- (“to scatter, to jerk”).

parole.significato: to space (to be separated to a distance)
parole.testo: From espaço (“space”) + -ar, from Latin spatium (“space”), from Proto-Indo-European *speh₁- (“to stretch, to pull”).
Borrowed from Latin spectātōrem, from spectō (“to watch”), from speciō (“to look at”), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ-.
From Old Galician-Portuguese espesso, from Latin spissus, from Proto-Indo-European *spidtos.

From Old Galician-Portuguese espiga, from Latin spīca (“spike”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *spey- (“sharp, sharp stick”). Cognate with Galician, Spanish, and Catalan espiga, Occitan espic, French épi, Italian spiga and Romanian spic.
Borrowed from Latin spīrāre.
Borrowed from Latin spīculum (“sharp point, dart”), diminutive of spīcum (“spike”), from Proto-Indo-European *spheh₁y- (“sharp, sharp stick”). Doublet of espicho.
Probably borrowed from Latin stilus (“stylus”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teyg- (“pierce”). Doublet of esteio (inherited) and style (borrowed from English).
Borrowed from Latin stimulāre.
From es- + Latin tremēscere (“to begin to tremble, to shake”), from tremō (“to shake, to tremble”) + -ēscō, from Proto-Indo-European *trem- (“tremble”).

parole.significato: structure (a cohesive whole built up of distinct parts)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin strūctūra (“adjustment”), from struō (“to construct”), from Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃- (“to spread”).
Borrowed from Latin sterilis (“sterile”), from Proto-Indo-European *ster- (“barren”).

parole.significato: stimulus (anything that induces a person to take action)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stimulus (“goad; incentive”).
From es- + vazio (“empty”) + -ar, from Latin vacīvus (“empty”), from vacō (“to be empty”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂- (“to lack; empty”).
Borrowed from Latin aeternus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyu- (“vital energy”).
Learned borrowing from Latin ēvacuō, from vacuus (“empty”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂- (“to lack; empty”).

parole.significato: to evoke (cause the manifestation of something (emotion, picture, etc.) in someone's mind or imagination)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēvocāre (“to call out, to summon”), from ex (“out”) + vocō (“to call”), from vōx (“voice”), from Proto-Indo-European *wōkʷs (“speech, voice”).

Learned borrowing from Latin executāre, from the past participle of exsequor (“to pursue, to execute, to accomplish, to examine”), from ex- + sequor (“to follow”), from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to follow”).
Borrowed from Latin exsūdāre (“to sweat out”), from ex- with sūdāre (“to sweat”), from sūdōris (“of sweat”), from Proto-Indo-European *swoyd- or *sweyd-.
From Old Galician-Portuguese falso, from Latin falsus (“deceived”), from fallō (“to deceive”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰwel- (“to lie, deceive”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fama, from Latin fāma, from Proto-Indo-European *bheh₂-mā-, from *bheh₂- (“to speak”).

Learned borrowing from Latin factor (“a doer, maker, performer”), from factus (“done or made”), perfect passive participle of faciō (“do, make”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, set”). Doublet of feitor. Piecewise doublet of fazedor.
From Old Galician-Portuguese fava, from Latin faba (“bean”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰabʰ- (“bean”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese favo, from Latin favus, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰōw- (“to swell, grow, thrive, be, live, dwell”).
From Latin favor (“favour; good will”), from faveō (“to favour”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰoweh₁ (“to notice”).

parole.significato: farm (a place where agricultural activities take place)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese fazenda, from Latin facienda, form of faciendus (“which is to do”), from faciō (“do, make”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, set”). Cognate with Spanish hacienda. Doublet of faina.

parole.significato: fever (high body temperature due to disease)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese febre, fever, from Latin febris (“fever”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷhris or *bʰebʰris.

parole.significato: to stink (have a strong bad smell)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese feder, from Latin fētēre, probably from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂-. Compare Spanish heder.
From Old Galician-Portuguese feo (“ugly”), from Latin foedus (“hideous”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyh₂- (“to frighten; be afraid”). Cognate with Galician feo, Asturian feu and Spanish feo.

From Old Galician-Portuguese feixe, from Latin fascis, from fascio (“to bundle”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰasko (“bundle, band”). Cognate with Galician feixe, Spanish haz, Catalan feix, Occitan fais, French faix, Italian fascio and Romanian fascie.

From Old Galician-Portuguese feliz, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin fēlīcem, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-lw-i, from *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suckle”). The Old Galician-Portuguese form fiiz, however, was popularly inherited, but later replaced by feliz, in a process of restoration.

Ultimately from Latin fēnum, monophthongized variant of faenum, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)-no-. Judging by the unexpected retention of /-n-/ (compare Old Portuguese fẽo), possibly borrowed from or influenced by Asturian fenu. The motive could have been to avoid homophony with feo (“ugly”), a

parole.significato: holiday (day declared free from work by the state or government)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese feriado, from féria + -ado, from Latin fēria (“holiday”), from Proto-Indo-European *dhēs- (“god, godhead, deity”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese ferida, from Latin ferīta, from ferītus (“struck”), from feriō (“to stike”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH- (“to pierce, strike”). Compare Italian ferita, Spanish herida.

parole.significato: to boil (heat a liquid until it begins to turn into a gas)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ferver, from Latin fervēre, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeru- (“to be hot, boil”).

parole.significato: fiber / fibre (single elongated piece of material)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin fibra. Compare the inherited doublet fêvera.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese filho (“son”), from Latin fīlius (“son”), from Old Latin fīlios (“son”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁y-li-os (“sucker”), a derivation from the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck”). Compare Galician fillo, Spanish hijo and Sicilian figghiu.
From Old Galician-Portuguese fim, fin, from Latin finis, of disputed origin. Perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- or Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd-.
From Old Galician-Portuguese fin, from Latin finis (“end”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰnh₂-.

From Old Galician-Portuguese foder, from Latin futuere, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to hit”). Compare Spanish joder, French foutre, Romanian fute and Italian fottere. Unrelated to Latin fodere.

Alteration of fouce. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fouce, from Latin falcem, from Proto-Indo-European *dhalk-, *dhalg- (“a cutting tool”). Compare Galician fouce, Sicilian fauci, Spanish hoz.

parole.significato: bellows (flexible container used to blow air)
parole.testo: From Latin follis, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolǵʰnis, derivative of *bʰelǵʰ- (“to swell”).

parole.significato: hunger (need or compelling desire for food)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese fame, from Latin famēs (“hunger”) (possibly through a Vulgar Latin alternative accusative form Latin *fam(i)ne(m), or more likely a variant nominative form *famen), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰH- (“to disappear”). Compare Galician fame, Spanish hambre (Old Spa
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fonte f, from Latin fontem m (“spring; fountain”), of Proto-Indo-European origin. Compare Galician fonte f and Spanish fuente f.

parole.significato: outside (on the outside of a building or location)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese fora, from Latin forās (“outside”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwer- (“door; gate”).
Borrowed from Latin frāgrantem.

parole.significato: brake (device used to slow or stop a vehicle)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese frẽo, from Latin frēnum (“harness; bit; curb”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer- (“to hold”). Cognate with Spanish freno and French frein.
From Latin frīgere, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer-. Cognate of Spanish freír, French frire, Italian friggere and English fry.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese frio, from Latin frīgidus (“cold”), from frīgeō (“to be cold”), from frigus (“cold, coldness”), from Proto-Indo-European *sriHgos-, *sriges-, *sriHges-. Compare Galician and Spanish frío, Asturian fríu, Catalan fred, Italian freddo. Doublet of frígido.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fruito, from Latin frūctus (“enjoyment, proceeds, profits, produce, income”), a derivative of Latin fruor (“to enjoy”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰruHg- (“to make use of, to have enjoyment of”). Compare Galician froito.
Borrowed from Latin frīgidus, from frīgus (“cold, coldness”), from Proto-Indo-European *sriges-, *sriHges-. Compare the inherited doublet frio.

parole.significato: soot (fine black or dull brown particles)
parole.testo: From Latin fūlīginem (“soot”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂li-, from *dʰewh₂-.

parole.significato: smoke (particles and vapor/vapour given off by burning material)
parole.testo: From fumo + -aça, from Old Galician-Portuguese fumo, from Latin fūmus (“smoke”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós (“smoke”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese fundo, fondo, from Latin fundus (“bottom”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn.

parole.significato: to pierce, puncture, make a hole in
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese furar, from Latin forāre. Compare Italian forare and French forer.
Borrowed from Latin fuscus. doublet of fosco.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fe, fee, from Latin fidem, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰidʰ-, zero-grade of *bʰeydʰ- (“to command, to persuade, to trust”). Compare Fala and Galician fe.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese galo, from Latin gallus (“rooster”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gelH-.

parole.significato: to freeze (become solid due to low temperature)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin gelāre, from gelu (“frost”), from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”). By surface analysis, gelo + -ar. Doublet of the inherited gear.
From Old Galician-Portuguese gelo, borrowed from Latin gelū, from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”). Displaced the inherited Old Portuguese geo.
From Old Galician-Portuguese gengiva, from Latin gingīva, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵyewh₁-.

From Old Galician-Portuguese genrro, *gẽero (“son-in-law”), from Latin generum (“son-in-law”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵm̥ros, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵem-. Cognate with Galician xenro, Spanish yerno, Catalan, Occitan, and French gendre. Unrelated to gênero.
From Old Galician-Portuguese gente, from Latin gentem, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁tim.

parole.significato: brother-german (a brother with the same mother and father)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin germānus (“of siblings”), from germen (“sprout, bud”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- (“to bear”). Doublet of irmão, which was inherited, and hermano, a borrowing from Spanish.
From Latin germen (“bud, seed, embryo”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- (“to bear”) + *-mn̥.
From Old Galician-Portuguese gola, from Latin gula, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷel- (“throat”). Doublet of gula.
From Old Galician-Portuguese grade, from Latin crātis, possibly from a Proto-Indo-European *krtis.
Borrowed from Latin gradientem, present participle of gradior (“to step, to walk”), from gradus (“a step, pace”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰredʰ- (“to walk, go”).

parole.significato: serious; grave (having possible severe negative consequences)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese grave, from Latin gravis (“heavy; grave”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷréh₂us.
Borrowed from Latin gravitātem (“weight”), from gravis (“heavy”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷréh₂us.
Inherited from Latin grūmus (“heap”), from Proto-Indo-European *gar-, *ger- (“to tie, bind together”).

parole.significato: edge (thin cutting side of a blade)
parole.testo: From Latin acūmen (“sharpened point”), from acus (“a needle, a pin”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”).
From Latin hasta, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰast- (“branch”).

parole.significato: to hibernate (to spend winter time in hibernation)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin hībernāre (“to pass winter”), from hībernus (“of winter”). Doublet of invernar.

parole.significato: kitchen garden, vegetable garden (garden for growing fruit, vegetables and/or herbs)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese orta, from orto, from Latin hortus (“garden”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰortós (“enclosure”), from *ǵʰer- (“to enclose”).

parole.significato: kitchen garden (garden for growing fruit, vegetables and/or herbs)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese orto, from Latin hortus (“garden”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰortós, from *ǵʰer- (“to enclose”).
Learned borrowing from Latin hostilitātem, from hostis (“enemy”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis (“guest, stranger”).

parole.significato: to ignore (to deliberately pay no attention to)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īgnōrāre (“not to know; to ignore”).

parole.significato: anger, rage (a strong feeling of displeasure, hostility or antagonism towards someone or something)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ira, from Latin īra, from Proto-Indo-European *eis.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese irmão (“brother”), from Latin germānus (“brother”), from the adjective germānus (“of true siblings”), from germen (“sprout, bud”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁mn̥ (“offspring, seed”), from *ǵenh₁- (“to beget, to give birth”). Cognates include Galician irmán,
From Old Galician-Portuguese juntar, from junto (“joined, together”), from Latin iūnctus (“joined”), present passive participle of iungō, from Proto-Indo-European *yewg-.
From Old Galician-Portuguese jurar, from Latin jūrāre, iūrāre (“to swear”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew-.

parole.significato: youth (quality or state of being young)
parole.testo: Probably a semi-learned term taken from Latin iuventūtem (“youth”), from iuvenis (“young”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuh₁en-.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese lagõa, from Latin lacūna (“pit”), from lacus (“lake; basin”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lókus (“lake, pool”). Doublet of lacuna and laguna.
From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from Latin glāndem, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelh₂- (“acorn”). Doublet of glande.
From Old Galician-Portuguese lasso, from Latin lassus (“weary; exhausted”), from Proto-Indo-European *led- (“slow; weary”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese lavar, from Latin lavāre (“to wash”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃- (“to wash”). Compare Galician and Spanish lavar, French laver, and Italian lavare.
From Old Galician-Portuguese leito, from Latin lectus, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ-. Cognate of Spanish lecho, Italian letto and French lit.

Learned borrowing from Latin lībertāre (“liberate, exempt”), from lībertās (“liberty, freedom”), from līber (“free”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ- (“people”). By surface analysis, liberto + -ar.
From ligar (“to unite; to bind”), from Latin ligāre (“to bind”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵ- (“to bind”).

parole.significato: to link; to connect; to join (to put things together so they work together)
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin ligāre, from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵ- (“to bind”). Compare the form liar, which may have (Old) French influence, as well as the inherited Old Portuguese form legar.
Borrowed from Latin līma.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese linha, from Latin līnea (“line, thread”), from līnum (“flax”), from Proto-Indo-European *līno- (“flax”). Cognate with Galician liña, Spanish línea and Catalan llinya.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese lynno, lỹo, from Latin līnum, from Proto-Indo-European *līno-. Cognate with Galician liño, Spanish and Italian lino, Catalan lli, Occitan and French lin and Romanian in.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, with metathesis from Latin lūcubrāre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk-. Cognate with Spanish lucubrar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese longo, from Latin longus, from Proto-Indo-European *dl̥h₁gʰós (“long”).
Learned borrowing from Latin longinquus (“far; remote”), from longus (“far, long”), from Proto-Indo-European *dl̥h₁gʰós (“long”).
From Latin labium (“lip”), from Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang loosely”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese lagrima, lagrema, from Latin lacrima, from Old Latin lacruma, dacrima, dacruma, from Proto-Indo-European *dáḱru-, from earlier compound *dr̥ḱ-h₂eḱru- (“eye bitter”).

parole.significato: wood (substance making up the central part of the trunk and branches of a tree)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese madeira, from Latin māteria, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr (“mother”). Doublet of matéria, a learned borrowing. Cognates include Galician madeira and Spanish madera.

parole.significato: magnificent (grand, elegant or splendid in appearance)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin magnificus (“great in deeds or sentiment, noble, splendid”), derived from Latin magnus (“great”), from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂- (“great”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese maior, mayor, from Latin maiōrem, from Proto-Indo-European *mag- (“great”) + *-yos (comparative suffix). Doublet of major and mor.
From maior (“bigger; greater”) + -ia (“-y”), from Old Galician-Portuguese maior, from Latin maior (“bigger; greater”), from Proto-Indo-European *mag- (“great”) + *-yos (“comparative suffix”).
Inherited from Latin malleus (“hammer; mallet”), from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese manco, from Latin mancus (“maimed”), from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂n-ko- (“maimed in the hand”), from *méh₂-r̥ ~ *mh₂-én- (“hand”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese margen, from Latin marginem (“edge, brink, border, margin”), from Proto-Indo-European *merg-.

parole.significato: but (introduces a clause that contradicts the implications of the previous clause)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mas, from Latin magis (“more”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂- (“great”). Doublet of mais.
Learned borrowing from Latin mātrīcem (“dam; womb”), from māter (“mother”), from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr (“mother”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese medir, from Latin mētīrī, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₁- (“to measure”).

parole.significato: member (one who officially belongs to a group)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese membro (displacing nembro), from Latin membrum (“member; limb”), from Proto-Indo-European *memso-, *mems-ro (“flesh”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese mente, from Latin mentem (“mind”), from Proto-Indo-European *méntis (“thought”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mentira, from mentir (“to lie”), from Latin mentīrī, denominal verb from mēns (“mind”), in which the meaning "to lie" stems from a semantic shift "to be inventive, have second thoughts" > "to lie, conjure up", from Proto-Indo-European *méntis (“thought”), from

parole.significato: shit; faeces (excretory product evacuated from the bowels)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese merda, from Latin merda, from Proto-Italic *(s)merdā, from Proto-Indo-European *smerd-h₂- (“stench”).

parole.significato: to put in; to insert into
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese meter, from Latin mittere (“to send, to put”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange, remove”).

parole.significato: milha, Portuguese mile, a traditional unit of distance equivalent to about 1481.5, 1851.9, or 2057.6 m depending on the…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese milha, from Latin mīlia, plural of mīlle (“thousand”) from its length of 1000 Roman paces, from Proto-Indo-European *(sm̥-)ǵʰéslo-. Cognate with Galician, Spanish, and Catalan milla.
From Old Galician-Portuguese mi, min from Latin mihi, from Proto-Indo-European *méǵʰye, dative of *éǵh₂ (“I”).

parole.significato: mode; way; method (method or manner of doing something)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin modus (“measure; manner”), from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese mole, from Latin mollis, earlier *molduis, from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥dus (“soft, weak”).
From Latin muccus, a variant of mūcus, from Proto-Indo-European *mew-k- (“slimy, slippery”). Doublet of muco.
Learned borrowing from Latin morbus, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *mer-. Doublet of mormo.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mormo, from Latin morbus, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *mer-. Doublet of morbo.
From Old Galician-Portuguese morte, from Latin mortem (“death”), from Proto-Indo-European *mér-tis (“death”), from *mer- (“to die”).

parole.significato: fly (various insects in the order Diptera)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese mosca, from Latin musca, from Proto-Indo-European *mus-.
From Old Galician-Portuguese mosto, from Latin mustum, neuter of mustus (“fresh, young", and, of wine, "unfermented”), from Proto-Indo-European *mus-, *mews- (“damp”).

parole.significato: to moo (to make a lowing sound)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese mogir, mugir, from Latin mūgīre (“to moo”), from Proto-Indo-European *mug-, *mūg-.

parole.significato: much; many; a lot of; lots of
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese muito, from Latin multus (“much; many”), from the Proto-Indo-European *ml̥tos (“crumbled, crumpled”, past passive participle). Compare Aragonese muito, Catalan molt, Galician moito, Italian molto, Romanian mult, Spanish mucho.

From Old Galician-Portuguese muller, moller (hence also Galician muller), from Latin mulierem (“woman; wife”), of uncertain origin. Maybe from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ- (milk; to milk). Cognate with Mirandese mulhier, Spanish mujer, Catalan muller, Italian moglie, and Romanian muiere.
From Old Galician-Portuguese mur, from Latin mūrem, from Proto-Indo-European *muh₂s. Cognate with Spanish mur and Romansh mieur.
From Old Galician-Portuguese muro, from Latin murus, from Latin *moerus, *moiros, from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to fix, to build fortifications or fences, strengthen”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese musgo, from Latin mūscus (“moss”), from Proto-Indo-European *mews-.
Feminine of médio (“medium”), from Latin medius, from Proto-Indo-European *medʰyo- (“between”).

parole.significato: average (constituting or relating to the average)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin medium, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between”). Doublet of meio, which was inherited.
From Old Galician-Portuguese moo, from Latin mola, from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”). Cognate with Spanish muela.
Borrowed from Latin natātiōnem (“a swim, swimming pool”), from natō (“to swim, to float”), from nō (“to swim, to float”), from the Proto-Indo-European *sneh- (“to swim, to flow”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese navio, from Latin nāvigium (“vessel; boat”), from nāvis (“ship”), from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us. Compare Galician and Spanish navío.

parole.significato: the practice of popes appointing nephews as cardinals
parole.testo: From nepote (“nephew of the Pope”) + -ismo (“-ism”), from Latin nepōs (“nephew”), Proto-Indo-European *népōts.
From Old Galician-Portuguese nervo, nervio from Latin nervus (“nerve; tendon”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)new-.
From Old Galician-Portuguese nobre, from Latin nōbilis (“noble”), from nōscō (“to know; to recognise”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃-.

parole.significato: name (word or phrase which identifies an individual person, place, class, or thing)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese nome, from Latin nōmen (“name”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥.

From Old Galician-Portuguese nomẽar, nomear from Latin nōmināre (“to name”), from nōmen (“name”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥ (“name”). Doublet of nominar, a learned borrowing. By surface analysis, nome + -ear.
Borrowed from Latin numerōsus, from numerus (“number”), from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to assign, allot; take”). By surface analysis, número + -oso.
Learned borrowing from Latin nuptiālis (“nuptial”), from nubō (“to marry”), from Proto-Indo-European *snewbʰo- (“to marry, to wed”). By surface analysis, núpcias + -al.

parole.significato: not; don't; haven't (negates the meaning of the verb or adverb)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese non, from Latin nōn (“no”), from Old Latin noenum, from Proto-Indo-European *né (“not”) + *óynos (“one”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese nevoa, from Latin nebula, from Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos (“cloud”). Compare Galician néboa and Spanish niebla. Doublet of nébula.
From Old Galician-Portuguese oytenta, oyteenta, oitaenta, from Latin octāgintā, variant of octōgintā (“eighty”), from Proto-Indo-European *oktōḱomt, from earlier *oḱto(w)-dḱomt (“eight-ten”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese oito, from Latin octō (“eight”), from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw (“eight”). Compare Galician oito, Spanish ocho, Italian otto, French huit.
From Old Galician-Portuguese olmo, from Latin ulmus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁élem (“mountain elm”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese olor, from Latin olōrem, a non-Classical counterpart to Latin odōrem, likely influenced by olēre (“to smell”), both ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed- (“to smell, stink”). Doublet of odor.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ombro, from Latin umerus (“shoulder”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃émsos (“shoulder”). Doublet of úmero.

parole.significato: English or American ounce, a unit of mass equal to 28.35 g
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese onça, from Latin ū̆ncia (“unit, ¹⁄₁₂ pound”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *óynos (“one”). As an English unit, a semantic loan of English ounce. Cognate with Galician and Spanish onza, Catalan unça, French once, and English ounce and inch.

From Old Galician-Portuguese ouriço, from Latin ēricius (“hedgehog”) (possibly through a Vulgar Latin form *auricius), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰḗr (“to bristle”). Cognate with Galician ourizo, Asturian oriciu, Spanish erizo (Santander dialect orizo), Catalan eriçó (dialectal oriç), Occitan eriç,

parole.significato: to hear (to perceive with the ear, without necessarily paying attention to it)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ouvyr, oyr, from earlier ouir, from Latin audīre, a compound of Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewis (“clearly, manifestly”) (from the root *h₂ew- (“to see, perceive”)) and *dʰh₁-ye/o- (“to render”). Cognate with Galician ouvir, Spanish oír, Catalan oir, Occitan ausir, French ouï

parole.significato: bakery (a shop in which bread and such is baked and sold)
parole.testo: From pada (“small loaf of bread”) + -aria, from Latin panata, from Latin pānis (“bread”), Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to feed, to graze”).

parole.significato: stepfather (husband of one's biological mother, other than one's biological father)
parole.testo: From Latin patraster (“father-in-law”), from pater (“father”), from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr (“father”). Compare Spanish padrastro.
Learned borrowing from Latin palātum (“palate”).

parole.significato: straw (a dried stalk of a cereal plant)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese palha, from Latin palea (“straw”), from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“flour, dust”). Cognate with Galician palla and Spanish paja.
From Old Galician-Portuguese parar, from Latin parāre (“to prepare”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“produce, procure, bring forward, bring forth”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese parir (“to give birth”), from Latin pariō (“to bear, to give birth to”), from Proto-Indo-European *perh₃- (“to produce, beget”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese parto, from Latin partus (“birth”), from pariō (“to bring forth, to give birth to, to produce”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to bring forth”).
Inherited from Latin parvus, from metathesized form of Proto-Indo-European *pau-ro, from *ph₁w- (“few, small”). Cognate with Galician and Spanish parvo.

parole.significato: pasture (land on which cattle can be kept for feeding)
parole.testo: From Latin pāstus (“pasture”), perfect passive participle of pāscō (“to feed”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to protect”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese paz, from Latin pācem, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ-. Compare Galician paz.
From Latin petītus (“sought”), perfect passive participle of petō (“to make for; to desire”), from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂- (“to fall; fly”).

parole.significato: fish (cold-blooded vertebrate animal that lives in water, moving with the help of fins and breathing with gills)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese peixe, inherited from Latin piscem, from Proto-Indo-European *peysk-. Compare Galician peixe.
From Old Galician-Portuguese pelar, from Latin pilāre (“to deprive of hair”), from pilus (“hair”), from Proto-Indo-European *pil- (“string of hair”). Doublet of pilhar.
From pele (“skin”) + -ar, from Old Galician-Portuguese pele (“pelt”), from Latin pellis (“pelt”), from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“skin”).

parole.significato: hair (filament which grows on the skin of mammals), except hair on top of humans’ heads, which is called cabelo
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese pelo, from Latin pilus, from Proto-Indo-European *pil-. The retention of single Latin /l/ in intervocalic position is irregular and may be the product of analogy with the near-synonym cabelo < Latin capillus.
Borrowed from Latin pelvis (“bowl”), from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“container”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese perna, from Latin perna, from Proto-Indo-European *tpḗrsneh₂ (“heel”). Compare Galician perna and Spanish pierna.

parole.significato: pitch (dark, extremely viscous material made by distilling tar)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese pez, from Latin picem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pī́ts (“pitch; resin”). Doublet of piche.
From Old Galician-Portuguese pimenta, from Latin pigmenta, form of pigmentum (“pigment”), from pingō (“to paint”), Proto-Indo-European *peyḱ- (“spot, color”).

parole.significato: sweet pepper, bell pepper (Capsicum annuum, an edible vegetable)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from Latin pigmentum (“pigment”), from pingō (“to paint”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peyḱ- (“spot, color”). Doublet of pigmento, a borrowing.

parole.significato: flat; level (having the same height at all places)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin plānus (“flat”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂-. Doublet of chão, porão, lhano, and piano.
From Old Galician-Portuguese pobre, poubre, from Latin pauperem, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w- (“few, small”).

parole.significato: poverty (quality or state of being poor)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese pobreza, from pobre (“poor”) + -eza (“-ness; -ity”), from Latin pauper (“poor”), from *pavo-pars (“getting little”), from Proto-Indo-European *pau- (“smallness”). By surface analysis, pobre + -eza.
From Old Galician-Portuguese podre, from Latin putrem, from Proto-Indo-European *puH-.
From Old Galician-Portuguese polpa, from Latin pulpa, from Old Latin *pelpa, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“flour, dust”).
Learned borrowing from Latin polluere (“to pollute, to stain”), from luō (“to wash, to cleanse”), from Proto-Indo-European.
From Old Galician-Portuguese *poombo, from Latin palumbus (“wood pigeon”), from Proto-Indo-European *pal-wo (“dark-colored, gray”). Cognate with Spanish paloma.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese porta, from Latin porta, from the Proto-Indo-European root *per- (“to pass through”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese portar, from Latin portāre (“to bring, to carry”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“go, traverse”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese poço, from Latin puteus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *paw- (“to strike”). Compare Galician pozo, Spanish pozo, Catalan pou, Occitan potz, French puits, Italian pozzo and Romanian puț.
Borrowed from Latin precem (“prayer; entreaty”), from Proto-Indo-European *preḱ- (“to request, ask”).

parole.significato: to nail (employ a nail or similar object as a fastener)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese pregar, a semi-learned term taken from Latin plicāre (“to fold”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleḱ- (“to plait, to weave”). See also chegar, an inherited doublet, and the borrowing plicar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese prea, from Latin praeda, from earlier praeheda, from prae- + Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“to hold”).

parole.significato: to arrest (to seize and take into legal custody)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese prender, from Latin prēndere, variant of prehendere (“to seize; to detain”), from prae- (“before”) + *hendō (“to take, to seize”) (not attested without prefix), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed-.
From prensar (“to press”), from Latin pressāre (“to press”), frequentative of premō (“to press”), from Proto-Indo-European *pres- (“to press”).

parole.significato: price (cost required to gain possession of something)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese preço, prez, from Latin pretium (“price”), from Proto-Indo-European *preti- (“back”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese prima, from Latin prīma, feminine of prīmus (“first”), from Proto-Indo-European *per-.
Learned borrowing from Latin proximus. Compare Spanish prójimo.
From Old Galician-Portuguese puro, from Latin pūrus, from Proto-Indo-European *pewH- (“to cleanse, purify”).
Borrowed from Latin pāgina (“page”).
From Latin pallidus (“pale, pallid”), probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pelH- (“grey”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese pan, from Latin pānem. Compare Galician, Asturian, Leonese, and Spanish pan, Catalan pa, French pain, Italian pane, and Romanian pâine.

From Old Galician-Portuguese quadrado, from Latin quadrātus (“squared”), perfect passive participle of quadrō (“to make square”), from quadrus (“square”), from quattuor (“four”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres.
From Old Galician-Portuguese quareenta, quaraenta, from Latin quadrāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwr̥(d)ḱomt (“four-ten”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese que, from Latin quid (“what”) (usurping as well the roles of Latin quod), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷid, compare *kʷís. Cognate with English who.

parole.significato: to break (end up or cause to end up in two or more pieces that cannot easily be reassembled)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese quebrar, itself, through metathesis, from Latin crepāre (“to crack, to creak”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorh₂-.
From Latin rēcta, feminine of rēctus (“straight”), from perfect passive participle of regō (“to rule”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- (“to straighten, to direct”).

From Latin rōbustus (“hard, solid”, literally “oaken, of oak”), derived from rōbur (“hard oak; hardness”), from ruber (“red”) (for its reddish hardwood), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rudʰrós, from the root *h₁rewdʰ- (“red”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese roer, from Latin rōdere, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *Hreh₃d- (“to gnaw, scrape, scratch”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese rogar, from Latin rogāre, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃roǵ-, ablaut of *h₃reǵ-.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese roin, ultimately from Latin ruīna or a word from the same root. Compare Galician ruín, Spanish ruin, Catalan roí, French ruine.
Learned borrowing from Latin ruptūra. Doublet of rotura, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Latin rēgula (“rule, bar”), from regō (“to rule, to guide”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ-. Cognate and doublet of regra (“rule”) and relha.
Deverbal from replicar (“to replicate”), from Latin replicāre (“to fold”), from re- + plicō (“to fold”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleḱ- (“to plait, to weave”).

parole.significato: flavour (the quality produced by the sensation of taste)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese sabor, from Latin sapōrem (“flavor, taste”), from sapiō (“to taste of”), from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁p- (“to try, to research”).
Borrowed from Latin sacrum (“holy”), from sacer (“sacred, holy”), from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂k- (“to sanctify, to make a treaty”).

parole.significato: to exit; to leave (go away from a certain place or situation); to get out (of)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese sair, from Latin salīre (“to leap”), from Proto-Indo-European *sl̥-ye-. Compare Galician saír and Spanish salir.

parole.significato: blood (vital liquid flowing in human and animal bodies)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese sangue, sangui, from Latin sanguinem m, from older sanguen, from *san-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁sh₂-én-, oblique stem of *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”). Compare Galician sangue m, Spanish sangre f, Italian sangue m, French sang m.
Learned borrowing from Latin sapientem, present participle of sapiō (“to be wise”), from Proto-Indo-European *sap- (“to try; to research”).

parole.significato: health (state of being free from disease)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese saude, from Latin salūtem (“health”), from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- (“whole, completed”).

parole.significato: sebum (oily substance produced by glands of the skin)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese sevo, from Latin sēbum (“tallow; suet”), from Proto-Indo-European *seyb- (“to pour out”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Latin siccāre, from siccus (“dry”), from Proto-Indo-European *seyk-.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese seco, from Latin siccus, from Proto-Indo-European *seyk-.

parole.significato: thirst (feeling the need to drink something)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sede (“thirst”), from Latin sitis (“thirst”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰgʷʰítis (“perishing, destruction, decrease”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese seguinte, from Latin sequentem (“following”), present active participle of sequor (“to follow”), from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to follow”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sẽo, from Latin sinus. Ultimately of Proto-Indo-European origin. Doublet of seno and sino. Cognate with Galician seo, Spanish seno, and French sein.
From Old Galician-Portuguese seis, seys, from Latin sex (“six”), from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs (“six”).
From Latin saxum (“a stone”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“cut”). Compare Galician seixo (“stone”) and Italian sasso (“stone”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Latin silva, from Proto-Indo-European *sel-, *swel- (“beam, board, frame, threshold”). Compare the doublet silva.

parole.significato: -less; without (not having, containing, characteristic of, etc.)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese sen, from Latin sine, from Proto-Indo-European *sene.

parole.significato: password (a word used to gain access)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese senna, from Latin signa, plural of signum, of Proto-Indo-European origin. Doublet of sino, senho, signo, and sina. Cognate of Spanish seña and Sicilian sinna.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese senhor m or f, from Latin senior, seniōrem (“older (one)”, “elder (one)”, used as a title of respect in Medieval Latin), the comparative of senex (“old”), from Proto-Indo-European *sénos (“old”). Doublet of sénior /sênior. Compare Occitan senhor, sénher, signou
Learned borrowing from Latin sēnsus (“sense”), perfect passive participle of sēntiō (“to feel, to perceive”), from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to head for, go”). Doublet of siso.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sentença, from Latin sententia (“opinion; sentence”), from sentiō (“to feel, to perceive”), from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to head for, go”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sentido, past participle of sentir, from Latin sentīre (“to feel”), from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to head for, go”).

parole.significato: to sense; to feel (to perceive by means of biological senses)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sentir, from Latin sentīre, from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to head for, go”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese serpente, from Latin serpentem (“serpent”), present active participle of serpō (“crawl, creep”), from Proto-Indo-European *serp-.
From Latin servus, from Proto-Indo-European *ser-wo- (“guardian”), or perhaps of Etruscan origin.
From Old Galician-Portuguese sesaenta, from Latin sexāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *sweḱsḱomt, from earlier *swéḱs-dḱomt (“six-ten”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese setaenta, from Latin septuāgintā, from earlier *septmāginta, from Proto-Indo-European *septm̥̄ḱomt, from earlier *septḿ̥-dḱomt (“seven-ten”).

parole.significato: sector; section (part, piece, subdivision of anything)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sectōrem (“cutter”), from secō (“to cut”), from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”).

parole.significato: oneself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, yourselves, themselves
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese si, from Latin sibi, from Proto-Indo-European *sébʰye, dative of *swé (“self”). Cognate with French soi, Italian sé, Spanish sí.

parole.significato: bramble (any of various thorny shrubs, especially those in the family Rubus)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese silva, from Latin silva, from Proto-Indo-European *swel-, *sel- (“mountain, ridge, forest”). Compare the doublet selva and Galician silva. The /i/ is puzzling. Philologist Leite de Vasconcelos felt that the word was not a Latinism and conjectured a term spīna *silvea wit
Inherited from Latin sonantem, accusative of sonāns. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swenh₂-. Doublet of sonante.

parole.significato: on; atop; on top of (located on the top surface of)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese sobre, from Latin super, from *eks-uper, which consists of Proto-Indo-European *eḱs (“out of”) and *uperi. Doublet of the borrowed super. Cognate to Spanish sobre, French sur, Ancient Greek ὑπέρ (hupér, “above”) and English over, super and sur-.

Learned borrowing from Latin societātem (“society, community”), from socius (“associated, allied; partner, companion, ally”), from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷ-yo- (“companion”), from *sekʷ- (“to follow”).
From Latin sopōriferum, accusative form of sopōrifer, derived from sopor (“sleep”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swep- (“to sleep”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese suar, from Latin sūdāre, from Proto-Indo-European *sweyd-.
From Old Galician-Portuguese sordo, from Latin surdus, from the Proto-Indo-European root *swer- (“ringing, whistling”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese sabio (“wise”), from Latin sapĭdus (“wise”), from sapiō (“to be wise”, literally “to taste of”), from Proto-Indo-European *sap- (“to try, to research”).

parole.significato: see (the cathedral and region under the jurisdiction of a bishop)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese see, from Latin sēdēs (“seat”), from sedeō (“to sit”), from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“to sit”). Doublet of sede. Cognate with Galician sé and Spanish sede.

parole.significato: European Portuguese standard spelling of sêmen
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sēmen (“seed; semen”), from Proto-Indo-European *séh₁mn̥. Doublet of semente and semilha.

parole.significato: series (number of things or events that follow on one after the other)
parole.testo: From Latin seriēs (“series; row”), from serō (“to bind together”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind, put together”).
Learned borrowing from Latin sēmen (“seed; semen”), from Proto-Indo-European *séh₁mn̥. Doublet of semente and semilha.
From Old Galician-Portuguese tal, from Latin tālis, from Proto-Indo-European *tód (“demonstrative pronoun”). Displaced collateral form atal.

parole.significato: tangible; touchable (able to be touched or felt; perceptible by the sense of touch)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin tangibilis (“tangible; touchable”), from tangō (“to touch”), from Proto-Indo-European *teh₂g- (“to touch”). By surface analysis, tanger + -ível.
Inherited from Latin tata, from Proto-Indo-European *tata-. Ultimately of onomatopoeic origin.
From Old Galician-Portuguese te, from Latin tē (accusative of tū), from Proto-Indo-European *twé, *te, accusative of *túh₂ (“you”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese templo, tenplo, borrowed from Latin templum, from Proto-Indo-European *t(e)mp-lo-s, from the root *temp- (“to stretch, string”).

parole.significato: time (the progression from the present into the future)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese tempo, from Latin tempus (“time”), from Proto-Indo-European *tempos (“stretch”), from the root *temp- (“to stretch, string”).
Learned borrowing from Latin temporālis (“temporal”), from tempus (“season, time, opportunity”), from Proto-Indo-European *tempos (“stretch”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese tẽero, from Latin tenerum, from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch, draw”). Compare its doublet terno.
Borrowed from Latin tēnsiōnem (“stretching; tension”), from tendō (“to stretch”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch, draw”). Doublet of the inherited tesão.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese termĩo, from Latin terminus (“boundary; end”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ter- (“through”). Doublet of término, a learned borrowing.
From Old Galician-Portuguese terno, from Latin tenerum, with metathesis (compare Spanish tierno), from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch, draw”). Compare with its doublet tenro.

parole.significato: third (one of three parts of a whole)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese terço, from Latin tertius (“third”), from trēs (“three”), from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tinger, from Latin tingere (“to dye”), from Proto-Indo-European *teng- (“to soak, dip”). Compare Galician tinxir.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese todo, from Latin tōtus, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *tewtéh₂ (“people; tribe”). Compare Galician and Spanish todo, Catalan tot, French tout, Italian tutto, and Romanian tot.
From Old Galician-Portuguese todos, from Latin tōtōs, accusative masculine plural of tōtus (“all; every”), from Proto-Indo-European *tewtéh₂ (“people”). By surface analysis, todo + -s.

parole.significato: thrush (one of several species of songbirds of the family Turdidae)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese tordo, from Latin turdus (“a thrush”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *trosdos.

parole.significato: to torture (to intentionally inflict unnecessary pain or suffering on helpless victims)
parole.testo: From tortura (“torture”) + -ar, from Latin tortūra (“twisting; torture”), from torqueō (“to twist”), from Proto-Indo-European *terkʷ- (“to turn”).

parole.significato: cough (expulsion of air from the lungs)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese tosse, from Latin tussis (“cough”), from Proto-Indo-European *tud-ti-s- (“cough”), from *(s)tewd-, from *(s)tew- (“to push, hit”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese touro, from Latin taurus, from Proto-Indo-European *táwros, related to Proto-Semitic *ṯawr- (“bull, ox”). Compare Galician touro and Spanish toro.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese traiçon, from Latin trāditiōnem (“a giving up, handing over, surrender, delivery, tradition”), from trādō (“give up, hand over, deliver over, betray”, verb), from trāns- (“over, across”) + dō (“give”) (from Proto-Indo-European *deh₃- (“to give”)). By surface an
From Old Galician-Portuguese tremer, from Latin tremere (“to tremble, to shake, to shudder at”), from Proto-Indo-European *trem- (“tremble”).
Borrowed from Latin tridentem, from trēs (“three”) (from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes) + dēns (“tooth”) (from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dénts, *h₃dónts).

From Old Galician-Portuguese trõar, from Latin tonāre (with an -r- due to influence from Latin tonitrus, Vulgar Latin *tronitus; see also estrondo and trom), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tenh₂- (“to thunder”). Compare Catalan and Spanish tronar.
Inherited from Latin truncus (“tree trunk; trunk of a human; cut-off piece”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from Latin trāns (“across, beyond”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₂- (“through, throughout, over”). Doublet of trans- and trans.
Learned borrowing from Latin tenuis, from Proto-Indo-European *ténh₂us (“thin”).
Learned borrowing from Latin terminus, from Proto-Indo-European *ter- (“through”). Doublet of termo.

parole.significato: tomb (small building or vault for the remains of the dead)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin tumulus (“mound; barrow”), from tumeō (“to swell”), from Proto-Indo-European *tūm- (“to swell, to increase”).

parole.significato: to howl, to utter a loud and mournful sound as dogs and wolves often do
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?] (compare Galician ouvear), from Latin ululāre, from a reduplicated Proto-Indo-European imitative root. Doublet of ulular, a borrowing.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese enguento (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), a semi-learned borrowing from Latin unguentum (“ointment”). Cognate with Galician ungüento.
Learned borrowing from Latin ūnīre (“to unite”), from ūnus (“one”), from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Indo-European *óynos (“one; single”).
Borrowed from Latin urgentem (“urgent”), from urgeō (“to urge”), from Proto-Indo-European *werǵ- (“to work”). By surface analysis, urgir + -ente.

parole.significato: to sweep (to clean [a place] using a broom)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese varrer, from Latin verrere. Related to the word guerra. Compare Galician varrer and Spanish barrer.
From Old Galician-Portuguese vẽa, from Latin vēna (“blood vessel”), of uncertain Proto-Indo-European origin. Compare Galician vea, Spanish vena, and English vein.
From Old Galician-Portuguese vela, an early borrowing from Latin vēla, plural of vēlum (“sail of a ship”), from Proto-Indo-European *weg (“to weave a web”). Displaced Old Galician-Portuguese vea.

parole.significato: fast; quick (moving or capable of moving with great speed)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vēlōcem.
From Old Galician-Portuguese ventre, from Latin ventrem, from Proto-Indo-European *wend-tri.

From Latin virga (“slender green branch, twig, stick”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *wisgeh₂ (“flexible rod or stick”). Compare Galician and Spanish verga, French vergue, verge. Doublet of virga.
From Latin vertīginem (“dizziness”), from vertō (“to revolve”), from Proto-Indo-European *wert-.

parole.significato: vertiginous (inducing a feeling of giddiness, vertigo)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vertiginōsus, from vertīgō (“dizziness”), from vertō (“to revolve”), from Proto-Indo-European *wert-.

parole.significato: to veto (to use a veto against)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vetāre. Doublet of vedar.
Learned borrowing from Latin vetustus (“ancient”), from vetus (“old”), from Proto-Indo-European *wétos (“year”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese vez (displacing vegada), from Latin vicis (“change, alternation”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyk- (“to wind, bend”).

parole.significato: vehicle; conveyance (device for carrying or transporting)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vehiculum (“vehicle”), from vehō (“to bear, to carry”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- (“to ride”).
From Latin vibrāre (“to shake, to agitate”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyb-, *weyp- (“to oscillate, swing”).
Derived from Latin vice.

parole.significato: someone who can see; someone who is not blind
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin videntem (“seeing”), present active participle of videō (“to see”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to know; to see”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese vigiar, probably a semi-learned term derived from Latin vigilāre, from vigil (“alert; awake”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵ- (“to be strong”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese vinte, vynte, viinte, from Latin vīgintī, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁wih₁ḱm̥ti, from *dwi(h₁)dḱm̥ti(h₁) (“two tens, two decades”), *dwi(h₁)dḱm̥ti.
From a semi-learned alteration of Old Galician-Portuguese vertude (based on its etymology), from Latin virtūtem (“manliness; virtue”), from vir (“man”), from Proto-Indo-European *wiHrós.
From Latin vivenda, feminine future participle of vīvō (“to live”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷeih₃w-. Compare Spanish vivienda; cf. also French viande (“meat”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese viço, from Latin vitium (possibly semi-learned), from Proto-Indo-European *wi-tio-, from *wei (“guilt, vice, fault”). Doublet of vezo, directly inherited, and vício, a learned borrowing.

From Old Galician-Portuguese voto, partly borrowed from Latin vōtum (“vow”), itself from voveō (“to vow”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁wegʷʰ-. Doublet of the inherited bodo (“food, money, or clothes given to the poor on holy days”) and boda (“wedding”).
Borrowed from Latin vulgus (“common people”), from Proto-Indo-European *wel (“to throng; crowd”).
From Latin vultus (“expression; face”), from Proto-Indo-European *wel-. Compare Italian volto (“face”).
Learned borrowing from Latin vulva, from earlier volva, from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn, wind”).
Learned borrowing from Latin vertebra (“joint”), from vertō (“to turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *wert-.
Borrowed from Latin victima (“sacrificial victim”).

parole.significato: you, ye (second-person plural nominative and prepositional personal pronoun)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese vos, from Latin vōs, from Proto-Indo-European *wōs.

parole.significato: vomit (regurgitated former contents of a stomach)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vomitus (“vomit”), perfect passive participle of vomō (“to vomit”), from Proto-Indo-European *wemh₁- (“to spew, vomit”).
Borrowed from Latin asperum, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂esp- (“to cut”).
Borrowed from Latin axis (“axletree”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs- (“axis”). Compare the inherited doublet eixo.

parole.significato: figure formed by two half-planes or two half-lines with the same origin; space limited by this figure
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin angulus (“corner; remote area”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂engulos (“joint?”).
Plural of óculo, a learned borrowing from Latin oculus (“eye”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃okʷ-. Doublet of olhos, which was inherited.

parole.significato: orbit (path of one object around another)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin orbĭta.
Learned borrowing from Latin optimus (superlative of bonus, literally “best”), from ops (“power to help”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ep- (“work”).

parole.significato: ovum; egg cell (female gamete in animals)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ōvulum, from ōvum (“egg”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm (“egg”).
Learned borrowing from Latin umerus (“shoulder”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃émsos (“shoulder”). Doublet of ombro.
Learned borrowing from Latin uterus.
